content: Coumarin is a chemical compound that acts as a toxin and is naturally present in various plants, particularly in high concentrations in tonka beans, woodruff, and bison grass. It has a distinct sweet aroma, often described as resembling the scent of freshly cut hay. Coumarin holds clinical significance as a precursor for several anticoagulant medications, most notably warfarin. Additionally, it is utilized as a gain medium in certain dye lasers. The term coumarin is derived from the French word coumarou, which refers to the tonka bean. In plants, coumarin is biosynthesized through a process involving hydroxylation, glycolysis, and cyclization of cinnamic acid. In laboratory settings, coumarin can be synthesized via the Perkin reaction, which involves salicylaldehyde and acetic anhydride. Another method of synthesis is the Pechmann condensation, which is used to produce coumarin and its derivatives. Several naturally occurring derivatives of coumarin include umbelliferone (7-hydroxycoumarin), aesculetin (6,7-dihydroxycoumarin), herniarin (7-methoxycoumarin), psoralen, and imperatorin. Both coumarin and its derivatives are classified as phenylpropanoids. Coumarin is frequently found in tobacco products and artificial vanilla substitutes. However, it has been banned as a food additive in many countries since the mid-20th century due to its moderate toxicity to the liver and kidneys. Its LD50 is 275 mg/kg, which is relatively low compared to related compounds. While coumarin poses only moderate danger to humans, it is highly toxic to rodents. Rodents metabolize coumarin into 3,4-coumarin epoxide, a compound that induces internal hemorrhage and can lead to death. In contrast, humans primarily metabolize coumarin into 7-hydroxycoumarin, a compound with significantly lower toxicity. Coumarin was officially banned as a food additive in the United States in 1978. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) classifies coumarin as a lung-specific carcinogen but states that it is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. In 1997, tobacco companies banned coumarin as an adulterant in cigarettes, but it continued to be used as a flavoring additive in pipe tobacco due to the absence of mandatory reporting requirements to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. In Europe, beverages such as Maiwein (white wine flavored with woodruff) and Żubrówka (vodka flavored with bison grass) are popular, but European health agencies have issued warnings against consuming large amounts of cassia bark, one of the four species of cinnamon, due to its coumarin content. Individuals with perfume allergies are advised to avoid coumarin. A company called Flexitral, based in Chantilly, VA, has developed an allergen replacement product named Coumane™ that is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). Compounds within the coumarin family include brodifacoum, bromadiolone, coumafuryl, difenacoum, ensaculin, and warfarin. Several of these compounds are widely used as rodenticides.
